title: APT: Animal Part Tracker v0.3.4

authors.name: Lee, Allen
authors.affiliation: Learning Through an Expanded Arts Program

abstract: APT is a machine-learning based software package that enables tracking the pose or posture of behaving animals in video. APT can work with potentially any animal (or animals), in any setting or experimental configuration. Its major functionality includes: Implementations of a number of leading DNN (deep neural network) architectures for learning and prediction, as well as extensibility to new, user-defined deep networks Support for GPU training and tracking on a local workstation with our Docker image, in the AWS cloud, or with the JRC GPU cluster (for Janelians) A fully-featured graphical interface A rich MATLAB command-line API for scripting and advanced users Support for multi-camera data with 3D-enabled labeling and tracking Support for projects with multiple animals and/or externally-generated body tracking ... and much more! More information here: http://kristinbranson.github.io/APT/ v0.3.4: Relatively stable version of the develop branch of APT, created 20220317.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

APT: Animal Part Tracker v0.3.4 shows clear scholarly uptake for a software tool focused on animal pose tracking. It has 11 citations in OpenAlex and 11 documented downstream reuses, with most citing works appearing as preprints and research articles in high-profile venues. The record suggests early but meaningful adoption, especially in neurobiology and insect behavior research.

Full narrative

APT: Animal Part Tracker v0.3.4 is a machine-learning software package for tracking animal pose and posture in video, designed to work across species and experimental settings. The impact record points to a tool that has moved quickly into active use: OpenAlex shows 11 citations, and the reuse graph also captures 11 downstream works that draw on the software. Most of those citing works are preprints, indicating that the tool is already shaping research in progress rather than waiting only for finished journal articles.

The citing literature is especially concentrated in neurobiology and insect behavior, with strong representation from animal behavior and locomotion research. The most visible citations come from venues such as eLife, bioRxiv, Cell, Current Biology, and Nature, which suggests that APT has been incorporated into work with substantial disciplinary reach. This pattern is consistent with a tool that fills a practical need in high-resolution behavioral analysis and can be integrated into multiple experimental pipelines.

The temporal pattern also supports a story of rapid uptake. Citations begin in 2023 and continue through 2024 and 2025, showing sustained attention after release rather than a one-time burst. The downstream works include both preprints and peer-reviewed articles, which indicates that APT is being used across the research lifecycle, from preliminary dissemination to published studies.

At the same time, the broader visibility record is modest outside scholarly reuse: there are no recorded online mentions in the supplied event-data sources, and the DataCite record shows no views or downloads in the digest. That does not diminish the evidence of academic use; it simply means the strongest documented signal here is citation and reuse within research rather than public-facing attention. The available record portrays APT as a specialized but influential software tool with clear uptake in the scientific community.
